headline_en: Bangladeshi expatriates in the Middle East in fear, families at home anxious too
summary_en: After Israel and the United States began attacking Iran on Saturday 28 February 2026 and strikes spread across the Middle East, Prothom Alo spoke by phone on Tuesday 3 March 2026 to 10 Bangladeshis in Qatar, Bahrain, UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, mostly from Cumilla. They describe fear, stopped work, falling customers, and a Qatar government instruction to stay indoors except for urgent need; one Bangladeshi is said to have been killed in Bahrain. The Cumilla district manpower office says the ministry has taken steps to protect Bangladeshis.

facts.statement: According to Prothom Alo (3 March 2026), Israel and the United States began attacking Iran on Saturday (28 February 2026); besides Iran and Israel, attacks have taken place in Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Cyprus, so that nearly the whole Middle East is at war.
In Qatar the government has instructed people not to stay outside for now except for urgent need, according to Doha-based Bangladeshi businessman Saleh Ahmed speaking on 3 March 2026.

A Bangladeshi driver in Doha, Ahmed Ulla, said that as of 3 March 2026 there had been no attack in Qatar outside the US base; he did not go to work on the first day of the attack on the US base and had been going to work for the last two days in fear.
Saleh Ahmed said that although Iran is attacking the US base in Qatar, debris is falling outside the base, which is spreading more panic among people.

Saleh Ahmed, a Doha businessman from Manoharganj, Cumilla, with construction, transport, tourism and housing businesses employing more than 200 Bangladeshi workers, said most of his business is outdoors, so only 10-12 office staff can work and only some of the transport workers are going to work.
Saleh Ahmed said he had a ticket booked to travel to Bangladesh on 6 March 2026 and did not know what would happen in the war situation.
One Bangladeshi has been killed in Bahrain during the Middle East war, according to Md. Selim, a Bangladeshi shop owner in Isa Town, Bahrain (no name or detail of the dead person is given).
facts.source_in_article: Md. Selim, shop owner in Isa Town, Bahrain

facts.statement: Md. Selim, who runs a car-parts and equipment shop in Isa Town, Bahrain, said businesses are open but customers are far fewer; Bahraini nationals stay home unless necessary, Bangladeshis go out to work out of necessity, and many are not finding work.

Abu Hanif, a Bangladeshi from Cumilla city living in Kuwait, said people there are afraid to go out to work, the situation became alarming within three days, and if it continues expatriates' income could stop or fall.

Prothom Alo spoke on 3 March 2026 to 10 Bangladeshi expatriates in Qatar, Bahrain, UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait; many of them have already had their work stop and they do not know when the situation will become normal.

More than 10 percent of Cumilla district's total population are abroad in various countries, and 80 percent of those expatriates are in the Middle East, according to the assistant director of the Cumilla District Employment and Manpower Office.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Atiqur Rahman, Assistant Director, Cumilla District Employment and Manpower Office

facts.statement: The Cumilla District Employment and Manpower Office assistant director said the ministry has taken necessary initiatives to protect Bangladeshis in the Middle East and he has learned more initiatives will be taken to keep expatriates safe; no specific measure is named.

headline_en: BNP manifesto promises a 'Probashi Card' for expatriates
summary_en: BNP's election manifesto, announced on Friday 6 February 2026 at Hotel Sonargaon ahead of the 13th national parliament election, promises expatriates a 'Probashi Card', membership of an expatriate welfare foundation, support on death, accident or job loss, easy-term loans up to BDT 10 lakh and an end to recruitment syndicates. These are party promises, not measures in force.

facts.statement: BNP's election manifesto (announced 6 February 2026, read by party chairman Tarique Rahman) promises a 'Probashi Card' for expatriates that will store their information, skills and job terms, be linked to a bank payment gateway with easy remittance sending, give extra incentive on remittance, and provide social protection to returned expatriates. This is a promise, not an existing service.

BNP's manifesto promises expatriate Bangladeshis membership of the 'Probashi Kalyan Foundation' (প্রবাসীকল্যাণ ফাউন্ডেশন), assistance on death, accident or job loss, access to SME and venture capital for entrepreneurs, jobs for returnees, education and health protection for their families, and help to go abroad again.

BNP promises to send one crore (10 million) workers abroad in five years, with training and allowances for people listed at upazila level, sending the poor abroad at zero or minimum cost, and easy-term loans of up to BDT 10 lakh.

BNP's manifesto says that under the previous government a handful of agencies monopolised manpower export through a syndicate, which sharply raised migration costs and left thousands cheated; BNP says it will stop syndicates and fraud in overseas employment and remove all barriers to manpower export.

BNP's manifesto promises hassle-free, respectful service for expatriates at airports and embassies, strict monitoring to secure expatriates' 'luggage facility' at airports, diplomatic steps to secure expatriates' rights, and infrastructure and quality changes to prepare workers for international labour-market demand.

headline_en: ACC case against 5 recruiting agencies for charging extra money to send workers to Malaysia
summary_en: On Thursday 13 November 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC/Dudok) filed a case against five recruiting agencies and their chairmen, managing directors and directors for collecting about BDT 314.35 crore extra from about 18,767 people sent to Malaysia. ACC says they charged on average five times the government-set fee of BDT 78,990.

facts.statement: The Anti-Corruption Commission (Dudok) filed a case on 13 November 2025 against five recruiting agencies and their chairmen, directors and managing directors on the allegation of collecting about BDT 314 crore 34 lakh 72 thousand 500 in extra money from about 18,767 people in the name of sending workers to Malaysia.
The government-set fee for going to Malaysia as a worker is BDT 78,990, according to the ACC; the accused agencies took on average five times that from each person.
The five agencies accused in the ACC case are GMG Trading Private Limited, The GMG Associate Limited, QK Quick Express Limited, MEF Global Bangladesh Limited and Dhamasi Corporation Limited.

Accused from GMG Trading Private Limited: chairman Mst. Monihar (51), managing director Monir Hossain (34), directors Md. Golam Mawla (65), Mozammel Hossain (30), Ismail Hossain (28) and Tasfia Maun (26).
Accused from The GMG Associate Limited: chairman Md. Golam Mawla (65), Walid Hossain Harun (44), directors Abdur Rahim (46), Nurul Amin (53), Ismail Hossain (28) and Tasfia Maun (26).

Accused from QK Quick Express Limited: chairman Rabiul Islam Robin (44), managing director Mohammad Munsur Bhuiyan (43), directors Mohammad Abdul Kuddus Bhuiyan (64), Rasheda Akter (39), Mst. Nilufa Kuddus (58), Aurangzeb Khan (65) and Mst. Shahina Khan (52).

Accused from MEF Global Bangladesh Limited: chairman Md. Altaf Hossain (54), managing director Md. Mokbul Hossain (56) and director Md. Haider Ali (53). Accused from Dhamasi Corporation Limited: chairman Md. Osman Gani (60), managing director Noman Chowdhury (62) and director Enam Ahmed Chowdhury (58).

headline_en: Human trafficking rises in the calm winter sea; preparation needed to prevent it
summary_en: At a meeting on Tuesday 2 September 2025 at the Cox's Bazar police superintendent's office, organised by Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association and IOM, speakers said sea-route trafficking from Cox's Bazar rises from October when the Bay of Bengal is calm. They cited 462 trafficking cases pending in Cox's Bazar courts, 21 departure points, and that most victims are Rohingya. No destination country is named in the article.

facts.statement: Cox's Bazar is described as a safe route for human trafficking by sea: after the monsoon, from October before winter, the Bay of Bengal is calm and sea-route trafficking increases; in the rainy season when the Bay is rough it stops.
facts.source_in_article: speakers at the meeting; Additional SP Md. Jasim Uddin Chowdhury

facts.statement: Sea-route trafficking from Cox's Bazar district takes place through 21 points in Teknaf, Ukhiya, Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar Sadar and other upazilas, according to the district police superintendent.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Saif Uddin Shahin, Cox's Bazar Superintendent of Police

facts.statement: 462 human trafficking cases were filed in Cox's Bazar district in the 13 years from 2012 to August 2025; they are pending in three separate tribunals and trials are delayed for various reasons.
facts.source_in_article: Safayet Bin Kamal, Case Management Coordinator, Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association

facts.statement: In the three months from July to September of last year (2024), 86 human trafficking incidents occurred in Cox's Bazar, most victims being Rohingya.
In 2023, 137 human trafficking cases were recorded nationwide in Bangladesh, and 44 percent of the victims were from Cox's Bazar district.
In 2024 more than 657 Rohingya died in 150 dangerous sea journeys undertaken for trafficking.

IOM Cox's Bazar identified more than 600 trafficking incidents (of a kind that could be filed as cases) in the Rohingya camps of Ukhiya-Teknaf in the past year, but cases are not being filed because of lengthy trials, out-of-court settlements, intimidation by offenders, lack of witnesses and lack of money.
facts.source_in_article: Arabi Mohiuddin Taher, IOM Cox's Bazar official

facts.statement: Cox's Bazar hosts camps of 14 lakh Rohingya refugees from Myanmar, which is why trafficking rings chose it as a safe zone; Rohingya girl children are the most frequent victims; trafficking has fallen somewhat compared to before but is not under control.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Saif Uddin Shahin, Cox's Bazar Superintendent of Police

facts.statement: The additional police superintendent said there is no research on why trafficking occurs or who is involved and no updated list of traffickers; there are 5,000 fishing trawlers at sea, and fitting them with a 'GPRS system' and putting trawler skippers in an online database would greatly reduce trafficking.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Jasim Uddin Chowdhury, Additional Superintendent of Police, Cox's Bazar

facts.statement: Rashida Khatun, district officer of the NGO Prottashi, said she recently presented 10 human trafficking cases in court and that trafficking is hard to stop unless traffickers and brokers are brought under the law.
Speakers warned that court delays leave offenders out of reach and make victim families reluctant to file cases, and that if human trafficking increases, manpower export will collapse.

headline_en: Relatives fear Zakir and his friend may have been killed by a broker ring
summary_en: Driver Zakir Hossain (24) and his friend Md. Mizan (38), both from Chatkhil, Noakhali, were found dead in a car in a hospital car park at Mouchak, Dhaka on Monday 11 August 2025. Zakir's family say he paid BDT 25 lakh about two and a half years ago to a broker ring from Lakshmipur and Feni to go to the United States, never went, and was threatened after asking for the money back; they suspect the brokers. Police have not yet determined the cause of death.

facts.statement: Zakir Hossain (24) of Lotkoria village, Khilpara union, Chatkhil, Noakhali paid BDT 25 lakh about two and a half years before August 2025 to a broker ring from Lakshmipur and Feni to go to the United States; the family says it holds all documents for BDT 19 lakh of the transactions. He never got to the US.

According to Zakir's family, the brokers kept stalling him with promises of taking him to the US; when he asked for the money back the relationship soured and the brokers threatened him; the money was supposed to be returned to him in Dhaka on Sunday 10 August 2025.

Police recovered the bodies of Zakir Hossain (24) and Md. Mizan (38) on Monday 11 August 2025 from a car in the car park of Dr. Sirajul Islam Medical College and Hospital at Mouchak, Dhaka; Zakir was in the driver's seat and Mizan in the back. Police had not yet established the actual cause of death.
facts.source_in_article: police; car owner Zobayer Al Mahmud alias Sourav

facts.statement: Zakir's mother Kulsuma Akter named the brokers as Fazlur Rahman of Lakshmipur and Sumon of Feni, among others, and said they received BDT 25 lakh and killed her son; this is the family's allegation and no case or arrest is reported.
Zakir had passed HSC from a Dhaka college, returned to his village, learned driving as preparation for going abroad and had worked as a car driver for one year.

headline_en: In Madaripur, paying extra to a broker makes everything 'right', otherwise there are 'mistakes'
summary_en: A report from the Madaripur Regional Passport Office finds applicants who use brokers pay nearly double the government fee and submit without trouble, while those applying alone are often turned back for 'mistakes' or missing attested NID copies. It lists the government e-passport fees for all categories and describes 17 unnamed computer shops outside the office whose staff act as brokers. The office's deputy director says the office is 100 percent corruption-free and has reported the shops to the deputy commissioner.

facts.statement: Government e-passport fees for a 48-page, 5-year passport: BDT 4,025 for delivery within 21 days, BDT 6,325 for express delivery within 10 days, and BDT 8,325 for super-express within two days.
facts.source_in_article: Department of Immigration and Passports sources

facts.statement: Government e-passport fees for a 48-page, 10-year passport: BDT 5,750 within 21 days, BDT 8,050 within 10 days, and BDT 10,350 within two days.
facts.source_in_article: Department of Immigration and Passports sources

facts.statement: Government e-passport fees for a 64-page, 5-year passport: BDT 6,325 within 21 days, BDT 8,625 within 10 days, and BDT 12,075 within two days.
facts.source_in_article: Department of Immigration and Passports sources

facts.statement: Government e-passport fees for a 64-page, 10-year passport: BDT 8,050 within 21 days, BDT 10,350 within 10 days, and BDT 13,800 within two days.
facts.source_in_article: Department of Immigration and Passports sources

facts.statement: Bayezid Munshi (18) of Majhkandi, Rajoir, Madaripur applied for a 10-year, 48-page ordinary passport (government fee BDT 5,750) but paid BDT 9,500 to a local broker as a 'full package' contract and faced no problem or questions.

Rubel Howlader (35) of Dasar upazila applied through one of the shops outside the Madaripur passport office; the shop asked BDT 10,000 for a 10-year passport and after bargaining took BDT 8,000, prepared everything, and he had no problem.
Shop staff outside the Madaripur passport office say they only fill in online applications and charge BDT 200 to 300 depending on type.

At the Madaripur Regional Passport Office, applicants without a broker are turned back if they do not have the original national ID card and an attested copy of the online NID copy; correction applications (name/identity) are often returned as containing 'mistakes'. Applicants with brokers were seen submitting directly at the counter.
facts.source_in_article: reporter's observation on Thursday 1 May 2025, 10am to 1pm

facts.statement: Akhtar Hossain of Tribhagdi, Kunia union, Madaripur Sadar, applied without a broker: he was refused first for not bringing the original NID, then told an online NID copy was needed, and the application was accepted only after he brought an attested online NID copy; he paid nothing beyond the government fee but suffered several trips.

Outside the Madaripur passport office there are 17 computer and stationery shops with no signboard or name on both sides of the road; every shop fills in e-passport applications and takes the passport fee, and all who work there are known as the office's local brokers. Brokers enter the office without identifying themselves while ordinary applicants must identify themselves to Ansar guards at the gate.

Three shopkeepers who did not want to be named said that before 5 August (2024) Chhatra League, Jubo League and other Awami-linked people worked as brokers there; after the political change they rented these shops, and 'everyone has to be kept satisfied' to operate.
The Madaripur Regional Passport Office started in 2020; in the six months from June to December 2024, 25,800 people received new passports there, and on average 200 people a day submit applications.

Madaripur Regional Passport Office deputy director Rotika Sarkar, newly posted, acknowledged brokers operating from the adjacent shops and said the deputy commissioner has been informed to take action; she claimed the office is 100 percent corruption-free with no link between brokers and the authority.
facts.source_in_article: Rotika Sarkar, Deputy Director, Madaripur Regional Passport Office

facts.statement: Anjuman Julia of Madaripur's Sacheton Nagorik Committee said passport offices are more transparent than before but people go to brokers to avoid having to follow the rules correctly themselves; she said people must become aware and the administration must act strongly for a broker-free office.
facts.source_in_article: Anjuman Julia, Sacheton Nagorik Committee member, Madaripur

headline_en: Two cousins missing after going to Saudi Arabia through brokers; case filed in court
summary_en: Cousins Sohel Molla and Iqbal Molla of Jaldia village, Rajbari went to Saudi Arabia about a year earlier after paying BDT 10 lakh to village neighbours acting as brokers, got no work and were tortured, and have been out of contact for three months. Sohel's wife filed a human trafficking case on 27 April 2025 in the Rajbari tribunal against Moniruddin Molla and Mamun Molla; the court ordered PBI Faridpur to investigate. The accused Mamun says the men refused to work and their passports were returned.

facts.statement: The family of Sohel Molla and Iqbal Molla (Jaldia village, Sultanpur union, Rajbari Sadar) paid neighbour Moniruddin Molla and his brother-in-law Mamun Molla BDT 6 lakh in cash on 5 March 2024 and BDT 4 lakh through a bank on 26 May 2024, a total of BDT 10 lakh, on a promise of good jobs in Saudi Arabia for the two men.
After arriving in Saudi Arabia, Sohel Molla and Iqbal Molla got no work and were instead tortured by the broker ring, according to the family.

On 7 February 2025 the brokers Moniruddin and Mamun took a further BDT 2 lakh from the family on the assurance of giving the two men work in Saudi Arabia; after that the men's contact with the family was cut off. The family says it has paid BDT 12 lakh in total.
After the two men went missing in Saudi Arabia, the brokers demanded a further BDT 10 lakh from the family, saying they would bring the men back if it was paid.

Rina Akter, wife of Sohel Molla, filed a case on 27 April 2025 in the Rajbari Human Trafficking Offences Suppression Tribunal against Moniruddin and Mamun under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act; the court ordered the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) Faridpur office to investigate and report.

PBI Faridpur superintendent of police Md. Rabiul Islam said he had learned the court gave the investigation to PBI but no papers had arrived yet; investigation would start as soon as the papers were received.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Rabiul Islam, SP, PBI Faridpur

facts.statement: Accused Mamun Molla told journalists that Sohel and Iqbal did not work at the company where they were given jobs and asked for their passports back; the passports were returned from the company through the agency, and he claims he has no further responsibility for them.

headline_en: 9 institutions and 7 individuals awarded at remittance fair in New York

headline_en: Record remittance before Eid; rising since August
summary_en: Bangladesh received a record USD 294 crore (2.94 billion) in remittance in the first 26 days of March 2025, more than any full month before, and bankers expect the month to pass USD 3 billion. The article gives monthly and fiscal-year figures, the BDT 123 ceiling at which banks buy remittance dollars, BMET worker-departure numbers, and economists' views that reduced hundi and money laundering after August 2024 moved remittance to legal channels.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the first 26 days of March 2025 was USD 294 crore (also given as USD 294 crore 50 lakh), the highest ever for any single month; daily average USD 11 crore 32 lakh. It was USD 133 crore or about 82.5 percent more than the USD 161 crore of the first 26 days of March 2024.

Bangladesh Bank figures for March 2025 remittance: USD 166 crore in the first 15 days; USD 225 crore by 19 March (USD 13 crore on 19 March alone); USD 243 crore for 1-22 March; USD 270 crore by 24 March; USD 294.5 crore in 26 days. The first week averaged USD 11 crore a day and the second week USD 12 crore a day.

February 2025 remittance to Bangladesh is given in the article once as USD 252 crore and once as about USD 253 crore, 17 percent more than a year earlier; January 2025 was 3 percent higher than January 2024.

In the first eight months of fiscal year 2024-25 (July-February) expatriates sent USD 1,849 crore, 24 percent more than the USD 1,493 crore of the same period of 2023-24. For seven months after August 2024 remittance averaged over USD 200 crore a month.

In Bangladesh Bank's monthly data for the last 5 years 9 months (69 months), March 2025 at USD 294 crore is the highest; the previous highest was December 2024 at USD 263 crore; since 2019-20 a total of 24 months exceeded USD 200 crore.

Banks in Bangladesh are buying remittance dollars within the central bank's ceiling of BDT 123 per dollar; competition among banks to buy remittance dollars has fallen and the dollar price stays within BDT 123. Earlier the dollar had at one time risen to BDT 128.

According to BMET, in the 20 years from 2004 to 2024 the most workers went abroad in 2023 (over 13 lakh), the second most in 2022 (over 11 lakh) and the third most in 2024 (over 10 lakh). In the first two months of 2025, 1 lakh 60 thousand workers went abroad.
facts.source_in_article: Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET)

facts.statement: People in the sector say a large share of workers who went abroad in 2023 and 2024 have now started sending income home, which explains the big growth in remittance.

CPD research director Khondaker Golam Moazzem said that after the political change the source countries of remittance changed markedly: the United States and United Kingdom have become the top remittance-sending countries instead of the Middle East, which should be examined carefully; reduced demand for money laundering and hundi may have raised legal-channel inflows.

SANEM executive director Selim Raihan said the challenge is to sustain the remittance flow after Eid and that barriers to sending remittance through legal channels must be removed; reserves are still not at a comfortable level.

Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserve under the IMF's BPM6 method was above USD 20 billion at the end of Tuesday 25 March 2025. The financial account moved from a USD 56 crore deficit in July-November to a USD 142 crore surplus at end-February; the current account deficit fell from USD 407 crore in July-February 2023-24 to USD 127 crore in the same period of 2024-25.
Before Eid-ul-Fitr in 2024, USD 45 crore in remittance came in five days, an average of USD 9 crore a day.

headline_en: Broker ring killed two Italy-bound young men from Faridpur, families claim
summary_en: Hridoy Howlader (22) and Rasel Howlader (22) of Kumarkhali village, Bhanga, Faridpur left home about two months before February 2025 to reach Italy through brokers and spent about a month in Libya. Their phones have been off since 24 January 2025, when the brokers said they were put on an Italy-bound trawler; on 31 January the families saw photos and video of their bodies, and say the brokers shot them and left them on the seashore. Police say they will act if a complaint is filed.

facts.statement: Brokers took BDT 16 lakh 50 thousand to send Hridoy Howlader (22) of Kumarkhali village, Gharua union, Bhanga, Faridpur to Italy via Libya.

Hridoy Howlader and Rasel Howlader left home about two months before 1 February 2025 for Italy through a broker ring and stayed in Libya for about a month; the brokers said they were put on an Italy-bound trawler at about 3am Bangladesh time on Friday 24 January 2025.

The two men's phones were off from 24 January 2025; on Friday 31 January 2025 the families saw photos and video of their bodies online (Hridoy's father says the brokers sent photos of the body on imo; Rasel's father saw his son's body photo on Facebook, lying on a seashore). The families claim brokers shot both dead and left them on the seashore.

After the men went silent, the brokers gave the families misleading information for several days, sometimes saying they were in hospital and sometimes that they had been caught by police; after the body photos appeared the brokers could no longer be contacted.

Bhanga police station officer-in-charge Md. Mokshedur Rahman said legal action would be taken if a complaint is received; no case had been filed at the time of the report. No broker is named in the article.

headline_en: Stipend for children of expatriate workers, apply quickly
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board has invited online applications from 25 November to 24 December 2024 for education stipends for children of expatriate workers who passed SSC in 2024 or HSC in 2023. The article gives the eligibility, minimum GPA by group, stipend duration, conditions and the application websites.

facts.statement: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board is giving education stipends to children of expatriate workers who passed SSC or equivalent in 2024 and are studying in class 11 or equivalent or a diploma course (first semester/year), and those who passed HSC or equivalent in 2023 and are studying in a university or medical college (first semester/year) in Bangladesh. Online applications run from 25 November to 24 December (2024).

Eligible for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend are children of expatriate workers who took emigration clearance through BMET's database or took Wage Earners' Welfare Board membership, and children of deceased expatriate workers who have received or will receive a financial grant from the Board.

Minimum results for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend: in SSC/equivalent 2024, GPA 5.00 in science and 4.75 in humanities and commerce; in HSC/equivalent 2023, GPA 4.80 in science and 4.50 in humanities and commerce. Children of workers who died abroad can apply with GPA 4.00 in either exam.

Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend: SSC-category students get it for two years through classes 11 and 12, or four years for diploma students; HSC-category students get three years for a pass degree, four years for honours and five years for medical. Session jam is not taken into account. The article does not state the stipend amount.

Applications for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend are online only (no in-person or postal applications), with scanned copies of required documents uploaded; the student's mobile number and a mother's/father's/guardian's mobile number must be given.

A Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend application is cancelled if the name in the expatriate worker's passport does not match the father's or mother's name on the applicant's certificate, or if information is incomplete or wrong; the authority's decision on awarding stipends is final.
To apply for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board stipend the notice gives www.wewb.gov.bd or http://stipen.wewb.gov.bd/stipend (as printed).

headline_en: Seafarers, pilots and cabin crew can buy as many Wage Earners Bonds as they like
summary_en: The Internal Resources Division issued a notification on Sunday 3 November 2024 lifting the investment ceiling on the Wage Earners Development Bond for expatriate Bangladeshis from 1 December 2024 and allowing reinvestment for two further terms. Non-resident Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew working for foreign-owned shipping and airline companies regain eligibility. The article sets out where the bond is bought, profit rates, tax status and the death-risk benefit.

facts.statement: By an Internal Resources Division (IRD) notification of 3 November 2024, from 1 December 2024 expatriate Bangladeshis can buy any amount of Wage Earners Development Bonds; the investment ceiling is removed, as it already was for the US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond.

Under the IRD notification, someone who buys a Wage Earners Development Bond with remittance income for one term gets reinvestment for two consecutive further terms, so investment can run for three terms totalling 15 years.

Non-resident Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew employed in the overseas offices of foreign-owned shipping and airline companies get the opportunity to invest in the Wage Earners Bond under the IRD notification.

Two months before the notification, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment wrote to the IRD secretary saying the ceiling on Wage Earners Development Bond investment should be cancelled or relaxed to increase expatriates' investment and remittance flow.
This article says the five-year Wage Earners Development Bond was introduced in Bangladesh in 1981.

Wage Earners Development Bonds can be bought at Bangladesh Bank, exchange houses, exchange companies, and the foreign and authorised dealer (AD) branches of scheduled banks; a foreign currency (FC) account is not required to buy them.
Profit on the Wage Earners Development Bond is income-tax-free and loans can be taken against the bond; it is a five-year bond paying simple interest.

The Wage Earners Development Bond can be bought by the foreign-currency earner (wage earner) personally or in the name of a person the wage earner nominates; government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad can also invest.

The Wage Earners Development Bond carries a death-risk benefit of 40 to 50 percent, paid to the nominee if the bondholder dies before maturity; it is capped at BDT 20 lakh, the bondholder must be under 55, and the nominee must apply within three months of the death. At maturity after the holder's death, the heirs get the principal and profit.

Wage Earners Development Bond profit rates: 12 percent on investment equivalent to up to BDT 15 lakh in foreign currency; 11 percent from BDT 15 lakh 1 to BDT 30 lakh; 10 percent from BDT 30 lakh 1 to BDT 50 lakh; 9 percent from BDT 50 lakh 1 to BDT 1 crore.

Under the Wage Earners Development Bond Rules 1981 (amended 23 May 2015) any amount could be invested; on 3 December 2020 the Internal Resources Division set a combined ceiling of the foreign-currency equivalent of BDT 1 crore for the Wage Earners Development Bond, US Dollar Premium Bond and US Dollar Investment Bond; on 4 April 2022 the ceiling was lifted for the two dollar bonds but stayed for the Wage Earners Development Bond, which also had no automatic reinvestment, forcing expatriates to withdraw earlier investments.

The Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association had long demanded this, arguing seafarers have no pension and cannot prove residence in one country.

facts.statement: A meeting on 15 October 2024 chaired by Internal Resources Division (IRD) secretary Abdur Rahman Khan, with Bangladesh Bank, Finance Division, Financial Institutions Division and Savings Directorate officials, decided to let seafarers, pilots and cabin crew invest again in the Wage Earners Development Bond after more than four years; the secretary said a notification would be issued soon.

In August 2020 the IRD and in September 2020 Bangladesh Bank issued separate notifications saying that Bangladeshi mariners, pilots and cabin crew employed by foreign-owned shipping or airline companies, and those appointed to overseas offices of Bangladeshi-owned shipping/airline companies and earning foreign currency, could not buy the Wage Earners Development Bond. Four state-owned banks had discouraged them since late 2019.
facts.source_in_article: IRD and Bangladesh Bank notifications as quoted by reporter

facts.statement: The opportunity to buy the Wage Earners Development Bond was never closed for any citizen staying abroad, government employees on lien, or people working at Bangladeshi embassies and high commissions.

This article says the five-year Wage Earners Development Bond was introduced in 1988 and that seafarers, pilots and cabin crew could invest for 32 years until 2020; the same article cites the 'Wage Earners Development Bond Rules 1981 (amended 2015)', and other Prothom Alo articles give 1981 as the start year.

Seafarers, pilots and cabin crew send their wages home through foreign banks or money exchanges, bringing about USD 60 crore a year into Bangladesh; the number of Bangladeshi seafarers is now over 12,000.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association

facts.statement: According to the Bangladesh Merchant Marine Officers' Association (BMMOA), seafarers have no pension, provident fund or post-retirement benefit; their contracts usually run 4 to 9 months; while on a foreign-flag ship a Bangladeshi marine officer is under that flag country's jurisdiction and cannot show proof of residence in any one country for the full service period.

BMMOA vice-president Golam Mohiuddin Kadri said they had made the demand for many years, the previous government ignored repeated letters, and restoring the bond would certainly increase remittance through legal channels.

Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul told journalists he had proposed cancelling the BDT 1 crore ceiling on buying Wage Earners Bonds, that Bangladesh Bank's help would be needed, and that more remittance would come through the bond.

facts.statement: The ministry's letter says expatriates' organisations have been demanding removal of the ceiling and that ambassadors and high commissioners have also written asking for it to be lifted.

facts.statement: This article says the five-year Wage Earners Development Bond was introduced in Bangladesh in 1981 and pays simple interest.

Profit on the Wage Earners Development Bond is income-tax-free and loans can be taken against the bond; it is a five-year bond paying simple interest.

The Wage Earners Development Bond can be bought by the foreign-currency earner (wage earner) personally or in the name of a person the wage earner nominates; government employees working at Bangladesh embassies abroad can also invest.

headline_en: Remittance has risen; USD 222 crore came in August alone
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh reached USD 222 crore in August 2024, after the fall of the Awami League government on 5 August, compared with USD 191 crore in July 2024 and USD 160 crore in August 2023. The article explains the July dip (bank closure, internet shutdown, calls to boycott remittance, gold-bar buying in the Middle East) and the new governor's widening of the crawling-peg band that lets banks pay up to BDT 120 per dollar.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in August 2024 was USD 222 crore, USD 31 crore more than July 2024 (USD 191 crore) and USD 62 crore more than August 2023 (USD 160 crore).

In January to July 2024 the highest monthly remittance was USD 254 crore in June, the highest single month in three years (the previous high was USD 259 crore in July 2020); the second highest of 2024 so far was USD 225 crore in May.

After Ahsan H. Mansur became Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024, the band for interbank foreign-exchange transactions was widened from 1 percent to 2.5 percent, so that under the crawling peg the dollar's mid price ranges from BDT 117 to a maximum of BDT 120; banks can now pay somewhat more for dollars.

Banks were closed from 19 to 23 July 2024 and broadband internet was off for 5 consecutive days and mobile internet for 10 days, nearly stopping foreign transactions; in the first week of August internet and banking were effectively shut and many expatriates announced they would not send remittance, then campaigned to send more after the government fell on 5 August.

It is reported as hearsay that in July 2024 many Bangladeshis in the Middle East turned to buying gold bars instead of sending remittance, hoping to get somewhat more money by bringing the bars home, sometimes with the possibility of a free return air ticket; when gold-bar buying rises legal-channel remittance falls.
Bank treasury officials said the competition to buy remittance at raised prices has eased and that reduced central-bank strictness has created a level field for all banks, increasing remittance.
Bangladesh received USD 21.61 billion (USD 2,161 crore) in remittance in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 23.91 billion (USD 2,391 crore) in 2023-24.

headline_en: Remittance is falling; will it fall further?
summary_en: Economic analyst Mamun Rashid's column (10 August 2024) discusses the fall in remittance to USD 1.91 billion in July 2024, the lowest in 10 months, amid the quota movement, bank closures and internet shutdown. He describes how hundi works and why exchange-rate controls pushed expatriates to it, gold-bar buying by Middle East expatriates, and Bangladesh Bank's push to banks to pay up to BDT 120 per dollar.

facts.statement: According to World Bank research and related surveys cited by the columnist, Bangladesh's potential remittance is USD 40 to 45 billion; former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal said only 51 percent of that comes through official channels, the rest being settled in local cash through hundi.
facts.source_in_article: Mamun Rashid citing World Bank and former finance minister

facts.statement: The columnist says the main complaint against hundi is that its foreign currency never comes into Bangladesh but stays abroad and is used for under-invoicing or money laundering; he says many exchange houses under common ownership with banks cooperated, giving expatriates advance loans and delivering higher taka amounts door to door.

Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 1.91 billion, the lowest in 10 months (the previous low was USD 1.33 billion in September 2023); USD 1.43 billion came on 1-20 July and USD 471 million on 21-31 July. The column says that in the first 3 weeks of the month 'on average USD 400 to 500 million' came (the averaging period is not stated).
facts.source_in_article: central bank report as cited by columnist

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 2.54 billion to Bangladesh in June 2024, the highest single month in three years; the previous high was USD 2.59 billion in July 2020.

facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank officials as cited by columnist

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank called in the managing directors of 12 leading banks and urged them to raise remittance; banks had been paying BDT 117 to 118 per dollar for remittance and were advised to pay somewhat more, so the remittance dollar rate recently rose to BDT 120.

The columnist reports as hearsay that Middle East expatriates rushed to buy gold: if they bring gold bars instead of sending foreign-currency remittance they get a little more money, and it also covers the return air ticket and even the fare from the airport to their village home.

Banks were closed 19-23 July 2024 and broadband was off 5 days and mobile internet 10 days, nearly stopping foreign transactions with Bangladesh's banks; in some places demands were raised not to send remittance.

Remittance averaged USD 22 to 24 billion a year in the last three years; during Covid in 2020 monthly remittance averaged over USD 2 billion and total reserves passed USD 48 billion; fiscal-year remittance was USD 21.61 billion in 2022-23 and USD 23.91 billion in 2023-24.

headline_en: 'Bankra', a locality transformed by remittance
summary_en: A feature (printed 22 July 2024) on Bankra in Jhikargachha, Jashore, where about 85 percent of families have one or two men abroad and remittance has built at least 30 multi-storey buildings known by the names of the countries their owners work in. Janata Bank's Bankra branch data show bank-channel remittance falling since 2019 while hundi rises. facts.statement: Bankra union in Jhikargachha upazila, Jashore has at least 5,000 families and over 19,000 voters; in 85 percent of families one or two men are abroad, so the union has at least 4,500 expatriates, according to the union parishad chairman.

facts.statement: Bankra bazar has one full Janata Bank branch, one IFIC Bank sub-branch and agent banking of 13 government and private banks; the Janata branch has about BDT 100 crore in deposits and 33,792 accounts.

About 30 years ago, after the government tightened controls on border smuggling in the 1990s, two or three men from Bankra went to Japan and later to the United States; others then tried to reach Japan illegally through brokers, but the brokers took them to Thailand and through the jungle to Malaysia. They returned after three years and themselves began sending people to Malaysia, which is how Bankra's migration started.

headline_en: Bangladesh has not fully met the minimum standards for eliminating human trafficking
summary_en: The US State Department's Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report 2024, released on Monday 24 June 2024, keeps Bangladesh on Tier 2: it does not fully meet the minimum standards but is making significant efforts. The report credits more investigations and convictions, victim-identification guidelines, an amended migrant worker policy and a first victim-compensation fund, but faults continued recruitment fees that leave migrant workers indebted, fines instead of jail for traffickers, and weak victim protection.

facts.statement: In the US State Department's Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report 2024, published 24 June 2024, Bangladesh remains on Tier 2 (not fully meeting minimum standards for eliminating trafficking but making significant efforts); neighbours India, Bhutan and Sri Lanka are on the same tier.

The TIP Report 2024 says that because the Bangladesh government continued to allow recruitment fees to be set, many migrant workers are falling into debt, which increases their risk of being trafficked.

The TIP Report 2024 says the Bangladesh government amended its migrant worker policy to increase oversight and accountability of recruiting agents, formally adopted guidelines for identifying trafficking victims, and identified more victims than before.
The TIP Report 2024 says the Bangladesh government for the first time set up a fund to pay compensation to victims of trafficking.

The TIP Report 2024 says Bangladesh increased investigations, prosecutions and convictions of traffickers, but courts fined most traffickers instead of jailing them, which weakened deterrence and probably created safety concerns for victims; no new anti-trafficking tribunal was established.

The TIP Report 2024 says victim protection in Bangladesh remains inadequate: officials often lack a victim-centred approach, shelters lack specialised services, and there are only a few shelters outside Dhaka, especially for male victims; cases involving exploitation of Rohingya refugees and internal trafficking (sex trafficking, forced child labour) were not adequately investigated or prosecuted.

The TIP Report 2024 recommends that Bangladesh, among other things, impose adequate penalties including significant prison terms, strengthen anti-trafficking tribunal staffing, improve protection services for all victims, monitor migrant-worker recruitment companies and brokers and enforce the law regularly, investigate credible allegations of Rohingya trafficking, and improve the quality of pre-departure training for migrant workers.

headline_en: USD 205 crore in remittance came in 23 days: Bangladesh Bank data
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank sources say expatriates sent USD 205.2 crore in the first 23 days of June 2024, ahead of Eid-ul-Azha, including USD 13.8 crore on 23 June alone. Bankers link the rise to the May increase of the dollar rate to BDT 117 (banks paying BDT 118-119 in practice), Eid, and possibly laundered money returning as remittance.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 205 crore 20 lakh to Bangladesh in the first 23 days of June 2024 (the month of Eid-ul-Azha), of which USD 13 crore 80 lakh came on 23 June alone; the headline rounds the one-day figure to USD 14 crore. USD 146 crore came in the first 12 days. In 1-21 June 2023 the figure was USD 166 crore 60 lakh.

Remittance to Bangladesh in May 2024 was USD 225 crore, the highest in 46 months, an average of USD 7 crore 25 lakh a day; the first 23 days of June 2024 averaged USD 8 crore 92 lakh a day, about USD 1 crore 67 lakh a day more.

In May 2024 Bangladesh Bank raised the dollar price by BDT 7 in one step to BDT 117, after which legal-channel remittance rose; although the documented rate is BDT 117, banks are buying remittance dollars at BDT 118-119, and the bank that pays more gets more dollars from expatriates.

Some in the banking sector say many people are bringing back previously laundered money in the name of remittance; an unnamed bank managing director said the budget allows whitening of black money, offshore banking allows bringing money from abroad, and the government has told many to bring money back.
Social Islami Bank, one of the top five banks by remittance received in the first 23 days of June 2024, attributes the rise to increased manpower export and the usual increase before Eid-ul-Azha.
facts.source_in_article: Zafar Alam, Managing Director, Social Islami Bank

facts.statement: Bangladesh received USD 2,161 crore in remittance in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,137 crore in the first 11 months (July-May) of 2023-24.

During Covid in 2020 legal-channel remittance averaged over USD 200 crore a month and total reserves passed USD 48 billion; after the dollar crisis that began with the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022, total reserves have fallen to USD 24 billion, with actual (net) reserves of USD 13 billion as of June 2024.

headline_en: Foreign minister congratulates Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: At a community meeting in a Madinah hotel on Thursday 20 June 2024, then foreign minister Hasan Mahmud congratulated Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia for sending remittance legally and obeying the law, according to a press release. He said about 30 lakh Bangladeshis are in Saudi Arabia and pointed to the expatriates' pension scheme and offshore banking.

facts.statement: About 30 lakh Bangladeshis are in Saudi Arabia, according to then foreign minister Hasan Mahmud speaking in Madinah on 20 June 2024.

Hasan Mahmud said a special pension scheme has been introduced for expatriates whose benefits can be taken even by people aged 55, and that expatriates have offshore banking facilities in which a dollar account can easily be opened.

Hasan Mahmud urged Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia to send remittance through legal channels, to obey the laws of the country they live in because an expatriate's crime gives the home country a bad name, and encouraged them to acquire business ownership abroad rather than only working in others' establishments.
The Madinah community meeting was attended by Bangladesh's ambassador to Saudi Arabia Mohammad Javed Patwary and the consul general in Jeddah Mohammad Nazmul Haque.
